issues.legal_issue: Capital sentencing requires separate consideration of the crime and the offender, followed by application of the societal rarest-of-rare test, rather than balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances against each other.
material_facts: The appeal concerned death sentences imposed for the murder of four members of one family.
The Court considered the governing capital-sentencing principles while determining whether the death sentences were justified.
issues.conclusion: The balancing of aggravating circumstances relating to the crime against mitigating circumstances relating to the offender is not the correct test. A death sentence requires the crime test to be fully satisfied, no mitigating circumstance favouring the offender, and, finally, satisfaction of the rarest-of-rare test based on societal perception.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684, Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P. (1973) 1 SCC 20, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470, Swami Shraddananda (2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767, Santosh Kumar Satishbhushan Bariyar v. State of Maharashtra (2009) 6 SCC 498, and Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2012) 11 SCALE 140, the Court held that crime-related aggravating circumstances and offender-related mitigating circumstances are distinct and cannot be reduced to a balance-sheet comparison. The crime test and criminal test must be considered, followed by a societal, non-judge-centric rarest-of-rare test.

rule.if: capital_sentencing_case and aggravating_crime_factors_fully_satisfied and no_mitigating_offender_factors and societal_rarity_threshold_met

predicates.capital_sentencing_case: The proceeding requires the court to decide whether a capital sentence should be imposed or upheld.
predicates.aggravating_crime_factors_fully_satisfie: The circumstances of the crime satisfy the aggravating-crime assessment for capital sentencing.
predicates.no_mitigating_offender_factors: No circumstance relating to the offender favours a lesser sentence.
predicates.societal_rarity_threshold_met: The circumstances meet the rarest-of-rare threshold assessed by reference to societal perception.

issues.definition: When a capital sentencing case satisfies the crime assessment, has no mitigating offender factor, and meets the societal rarity threshold, the rule permits a capital sentence.

issues.legal_issue: The death sentence was not warranted where the offenders' age and the possibility of their reformation and rehabilitation were mitigating circumstances, despite the grave circumstances of the murders.
material_facts: The offenders were 34 and 22 years old at the time of the murders.
The Court considered the possibility that they could be reformed and rehabilitated.
They had caused the deaths of four people, including a family and two children, in the presence of the surviving eyewitness.
The murders arose from a family property dispute.
The Court found that the totality of the circumstances did not warrant capital punishment.
issues.conclusion: The Court substituted life imprisonment for the death sentences and directed that the offenders serve a minimum term without remission.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the capital-sentencing principles in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470, and Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2012) 11 SCALE 140, the Court treated age and the probability of reformation and rehabilitation as relevant mitigating circumstances. It also relied on Sandeep v. State of U.P. (2012) 6 SCC 107 in fixing a minimum period of imprisonment as part of the life sentence.

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a death sentence.
predicates.mitigating_circumstances_present: The offender's age or another circumstance relating to the offender favours a lesser sentence.
predicates.rehabilitation_possible: The possibility that the offender can be reformed and rehabilitated has not been ruled out.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a death sentence, the presence of mitigating circumstances and a possibility of rehabilitation results in replacement of the death sentence with life imprisonment subject to a minimum non-remittable term.

issues.legal_issue: The convictions for murder based on the evidence accepted by the courts below did not warrant appellate interference.
material_facts: An eyewitness described the armed attack and identified the assailants.
Medical evidence established that the victims died from injuries including severance of neck structures.
The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellants, and the Supreme Court reviewed the oral and documentary evidence.
The appellants' arguments before the Supreme Court were focused primarily on sentence.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no ground to disturb the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: The convictions were for murder read with common intention under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. On review of the oral and documentary evidence, the Court found no basis to upset the concurrent findings of the courts below.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_supported_by_medical_: An eyewitness account of the crime is supported by medical evidence concerning the victims' injuries or deaths.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the appellate court below have both found the accused guilty.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction appeal, an eyewitness account supported by medical evidence and concurrent findings of guilt results in the conviction being upheld.
